paragraphs: One-sentence judgment: hairdressers, hairstylists, and cosmetologists are not “people who just cut according to the picture,” but salon positions that first communicate with and observe the condition of hair and scalp, analyze hair quality and face shape, and then provide styling and care plans: cutting and trimming and shaping hair, shampooing and rinsing and conditioning and drying, bleaching and dyeing and toning, applying water or setting or straightening or permanent waving solutions and pressing curls with curling irons and hot combs and curling wands, massaging and treating the scalp, combing and spraying to set, shaping eyebrows and removing facial hair, and keeping the workbench clean and disinfecting tools such as scissors and combs and maintaining customer information records; it is not suitable for people who only want to improvise by feel, are unwilling to first confirm customer requirements and ask about skin and allergies, and are unwilling to treat tool disinfection, workstation cleaning, and product label verification as part of the job.

Signals to keep exploring: you are willing to first repeat back the effect the customer wants and observe the scalp, hair, and skin; you can stay steady in the rhythm of prolonged standing and fine hand control; you take the initiative to verify product labels and contact times and follow the materials and procedures; you are willing to stop and confirm first when a customer changes requirements or a skin or scalp abnormality appears; and you can truthfully record services, products, and exceptions.

Conditions for pausing investment first: you have not yet completed a full consultation-and-observation—cutting, dyeing, permanent waving, and styling—disinfection and cleaning—recording loop under any supervised conditions, or you can only explain your interest by saying “I like doing styling”; also do not treat having done hair for family and friends or having dyed hair at home as proof that you can independently mix chemical products, handle a customer's skin or scalp abnormality on your own, or independently bear venue hygiene responsibility. Tool disinfection and skin barrier, chemical product and dyeing and permanent waving and formaldehyde exposure control, product label and contact time verification, customer image and health information handling, and practice and salon authorization must be carried out in accordance with the applicable jurisdiction, the competent authority, and employer systems and must leave traceable records; this page does not provide any cutting, dyeing, or permanent waving formulas, contact times, or work instructions.

Education and practice licensure are two different tracks: O*NET lists 39-5012.00 as Job Zone Three (SVP 6.0 to <7.0), and the page “does not publish the percentage at each education level,” listing only three categories (some jobs require a postsecondary certificate, some require a high school diploma or equivalent, and some require having attended college without a degree); the BLS Occupational Outlook Handbook lists the typical entry-level education for this occupational group as a postsecondary nondegree award, with no related work experience required and no on-the-job training, and notes that every U.S. state requires licensure, usually requiring graduation from a state-approved cosmetology or beauty program and passing an examination. Education, occupational training, state practice licensure, employer hiring and salon authorization, and job-level authorization for chemical product and instrument use are different statuses and must be verified item by item according to state and employer and position; this occupation and barbers 39-5011.00 are separate adjacent codes, and licensing scope varies by jurisdiction.

In one sentence: this is a service position that delivers steadily in a rhythm of first communicating and observing and then working through prolonged standing, fine hand control, and chemical exposure, with the core being cutting, dyeing, permanent waving, styling, scalp care, tool disinfection, and records — not an interest in fashion or an imagination about social media.

The work of hairdressers, hairstylists, and cosmetologists can be divided into three categories: cutting, dyeing, permanent waving, and styling services (analyzing customers' hair and other physical features and recommending beauty care or hairstyles; cutting and trimming and shaping hair or hairpieces according to customer requirements and hair quality and facial features using clippers, scissors, trimmers, and razors; shampooing and rinsing and conditioning and drying hair and scalp or hairpieces with water and shampoo or other solutions; bleaching and dyeing and toning with applicators or brushes; applying water or setting or straightening or permanent waving solutions and pressing curls with rollers, curling irons, hot combs, and curling wands; massaging and treating the scalp with hands and fingers or vibrating equipment for hygiene and therapeutic purposes; combing and brushing and spraying hair or wigs to set them; shaping eyebrows and removing facial hair); hygiene and safety and records (keeping the workbench clean and disinfecting tools such as scissors and combs; updating and maintaining customer information records; operating a cash register to receive payments; ordering and displaying and maintaining supplies); and salon affairs and sales (developing new styles and techniques; demonstrating and selling hair care products and cosmetics; recommending and explaining the use of cosmetics, lotions, and creams; training or supervising other stylists and hairdressers and assistants; applying therapeutic agents as authorized and advising customers to seek medical care for chronic or infectious scalp problems). All three categories presume stopping to verify first when customer requirements are unclear, when product labels or tool conditions are unknown, or when a skin or scalp abnormality or allergic reaction appears.

O*NET occupational identity and tasks: O*NET 39-5012.00 Hairdressers, Hairstylists, and Cosmetologists (page updated 2026, Bright Outlook). The official duties are to provide beauty services, including cutting and dyeing and styling hair and massaging and treating the scalp, and may also include shampooing, makeup, arranging wigs, hair removal, and providing nail and skin care services; there are 20 official tasks (14 core and 6 supplemental), with core task importance scores from 95 to 71 and supplemental tasks from 81 to 48. The work activities page lists 41 items with importance scores, the highest being performing for or working directly with the public 82, establishing and maintaining interpersonal relationships 75, persuading others to buy merchandise or change their minds or behavior 75, assisting and caring for others 73, updating and using relevant knowledge 73, thinking creatively 71, making decisions and solving problems 70, resolving conflicts and negotiating with others 66, getting information 65, communicating with people outside the organization 64, organizing, planning, and prioritizing work 64, and training and teaching others 64. There are 21 detailed work activities (no scores). The task list describes group work and does not mean every position performs all tasks. Barbers 39-5011.00 is a separate adjacent code.

entries: Communication and observation | Give the service a basis | Analyze the customer's hair and other physical features, and confirm the desired styling and care plan and the limiting conditions before starting.

Cutting and shaping | Give the output a specification | Cut and trim and shape hair or hairpieces according to customer requirements and hair quality and facial features using clippers, scissors, trimmers, and razors.

Dyeing, permanent waving, and styling | Make the result reproducible | Bleach and dye and tone with applicators or brushes, apply water or setting or straightening or permanent waving solutions and control contact time according to the instructions, and press curls and comb and set using rollers, curling irons, hot combs, and curling wands.

Scalp and skin care | Keep care within scope | Massage and treat the scalp as authorized, shape eyebrows and remove facial hair, and advise the customer to seek medical care when there is an abnormality.

Tool disinfection and workstation cleaning | Keep risk controlled | Keep the workbench clean and disinfect tools such as scissors and combs, handle contaminated items and chemicals and waste, and maintain ventilation.

Records, charging, and sales | Make the process traceable | Update and maintain customer information records, operate the cash register to receive payments, order and display and maintain supplies, and demonstrate and sell hair care products and cosmetics within the authorized scope.

paragraphs:
Work environment | 88% continuously or almost continuously make repetitive motions, 71% continuously or almost continuously stand, 30% continuously or almost continuously bend or twist the body, and 54% continuously or almost continuously keep or regain balance; 94% have face-to-face discussions every day, 88% are in contact with others continuously, 88% work very close (within touching distance) to others, and 71% have telephone conversations every day; 42% are exposed to contaminants (dust, gases, and odors) every day, 38% are exposed to minor burns, cuts, bites, or stings every day, 26% are in hazardous conditions every day (64% never), 17% are exposed to disease or infections every day (65% never), and 18% are exposed to distracting or uncomfortable noise every day; 74% wear common protective or safety equipment every day and 11% wear specialized protective equipment every day; 58% never kneel, crouch, or crawl and 85% never climb ladders.
Main equipment and tools | Scissors and clippers and combs and razors and hair dryers and curling irons and hot combs and curling wands, dyeing, permanent waving, setting, and care products and developers and toning supplies, workbenches and disinfection and cleaning supplies, cash register and appointment and customer file tools, and personal protection (gloves, aprons, face shields, and ventilation arrangements as the work requires).
Task rhythm | 96% have a regular schedule; 19% have a typical workweek exceeding 40 hours and 13% work 40 hours; 43% face time pressure every day; 94% consider the pace determined by equipment speed not at all important; 89% have a lot of freedom in decisions and 94% have a lot of freedom in determining tasks, priorities, and goals; 61% make decisions every day; 60% consider the work not at all automated.
Collaboration | Collaborate with stylists, assistants, and front-desk colleagues in the same salon; 48% consider working with a work group or team extremely important (another 30% very important), 28% bear high responsibility for the health and safety of others, and 85% consider dealing with external customers or the public extremely important (another 15% very important).
Competition and pressure | 38% are in conflict situations at least once a week and 17% deal with unpleasant or angry people at least once a week (88% never encounter people with violent behavior); 39% consider the consequences of error serious (37% consider them not at all serious); 20% consider competition extremely fierce (another 22% highly fierce and 26% moderately fierce).
Compliance and safety | Cutting, dyeing, permanent waving, tool disinfection, chemicals, and ventilation must meet applicable hygiene and occupational safety requirements; on the U.S. side, OSHA notes that some hair smoothing and straightening products may contain formaldehyde or release it when used (heated), and its formaldehyde standard and hazard communication standard apply (air testing, ventilation, protective equipment, and training); the FDA notes that products for cleansing and beautifying purposes are generally regulated as cosmetics (including shampoos, permanent wave solutions, and hair dyes), and, except for color additives (other than coal-tar hair dyes), premarket approval does not apply, with product and ingredient safety the responsibility of the company.
Records and retrospective | Service items and the tools and products and contact times used, skin and allergy inquiry results, tool cleaning and disinfection handling, and customer feedback and charges and exceptions need to be traceable.
Skills and training | O*NET lists this occupation as Job Zone Three (SVP 6.0 to <7.0); basic skills are led by active listening 72, speaking 69, critical thinking 60, active learning 56, monitoring 50, and reading comprehension 50; transferable skills are led by service orientation 66, judgment and decision making 56, social perceptiveness 53, complex problem solving 50, time management 50, coordination 47, instructing 47, and persuasion 47; the knowledge fields publish customer and personal service 94 and sales and marketing 81; the current page already lists abilities such as near vision, arm steadiness, and finger dexterity and work styles such as social orientation, dependability, cooperation, and attention to detail, none of which are individual admission scores.
Entry and authorization | Education and training do not equal a state practice license or employer hiring; on the U.S. side every state requires licensure, usually requiring completion of a state-approved program and passing an examination; the licensing scope of this occupation and barbers 39-5011.00 varies by jurisdiction.
Industry and employers | The O*NET industry distribution is other services (except public administration) 45% and other industries (including retail trade) 55%; common employers are chain or independent salons, community hair salons, and hotel, resort, and comprehensive beauty establishments.
Cutting, dyeing, permanent waving, and styling services

U.S. wage distribution: the 2025 BLS Occupational Employment and Wage Statistics (OEWS) displayed by O*NET give, under this occupation's 39-5012.00 definition, annual salaries of 27,040 USD at the 10th percentile, 30,120 USD at the 25th percentile, 35,790 USD at the median, 48,830 USD at the 75th percentile, and 71,190 USD at the 90th percentile; hourly wages of 13.00 USD at the 10th percentile, 14.48 USD at the 25th percentile, 17.21 USD at the median, 23.48 USD at the 75th percentile, and 34.23 USD at the 90th percentile. The O*NET page does not state that these data are taken from another occupation; they are for this occupational definition; the Pay section of the BLS Occupational Outlook Handbook chapter separately lists this occupation's May 2025 median hourly wage of 17.21 USD, which is consistent. The median does not equal an entry-level wage and does not constitute an income promise; OEWS includes commissions, production bonuses, and tips and excludes overtime premiums and self-employment income.

Communicate with and observe the condition of hair and scalp → analyze hair quality and face shape and recommend a plan → verify product labels and ask about skin and allergies → cut and trim and shape and dye or curl → monitor the process and confirm the result → disinfect tools and clean the workstation and record services and charges.

The occupational profile of the China Employment Training Technical Instruction Center specifies hairdresser 4-10-03-02: using hairdressing tools to design, trim, and create customer hairstyles, including washing, cutting, dyeing and permanent waving, hair setting, and scalp care. It can be compared with the hair services on this page, but it cannot be used to equate one-to-one with all beauty services of U.S. 39-5012. Insufficient evidence: a precise national wage median and percentiles for this combined occupation in mainland China. The urban unit average for the residents' services industry may be referenced and must be kept separate from occupational wages.
Hygiene and safety and records

Employment and prospects: the BLS data displayed by O*NET give, under this occupation's 39-5012.00 definition, about 595,000 employed in 2025 and about 640,900 in 2035 (2025—2035 +8%, labeled much faster than average (8%)), with about 73,400 job openings per year over the projection period. The corresponding chapter of the BLS Occupational Outlook Handbook is the combined “Barbers, Hairstylists, and Cosmetologists” definition: 670,800 employed in 2025, 2025—2035 +7% (much faster than average), a change of +48,400, and about 80,300 annual openings (mostly from replacement needs); the combined definition covers the three groups of barbers, hairstylists, and cosmetologists and cannot be treated as this occupation's separate definition.

Confirm the condition of the workbench and tools → clean and disinfect tools such as scissors and combs according to procedure → verify product labels and ingredients and contact times → maintain ventilation and wear the corresponding protection → isolate contaminated items and handle chemicals and waste → record disinfection, product use, and exceptions.

Industry distribution and tool signals: the current O*NET industry distribution gives other services (except public administration) 45% and other industries (including retail trade) 55% — the page publishes under the two categories “other services” and “other industries” and does not give a finer industry category breakdown. Sample job titles include Beautician, Beauty Specialist, Cosmetologist, Hair Artist, Hair Dresser, Hair Stylist, Hairdresser, Hairstylist, Lash Technician, and Stylist. On posting technology signals, O*NET lists 6 technology skills and marks them as hot technologies (Microsoft Office, Microsoft Excel, and Microsoft Word each appear at below 1%; Apple iOS, Facebook, and Intuit QuickBooks have no published rates). These come from job posting text and do not represent job adoption rates or degree of automation.

Collaborate with stylists, assistants, and front-desk colleagues in the same salon; where tool disinfection and skin barrier, chemical products and dyeing and permanent waving and formaldehyde exposure, product labels and contact times, customer image and health information, and scope of practice and salon authorization are involved, act in accordance with the applicable jurisdiction, the competent authority, and employer systems, do not decide on your own, and stop and report when a skin or scalp abnormality or allergic reaction occurs or the condition of a product is unknown.

Hairdressers, hairstylists, and cosmetologists focus on comprehensive beauty services of cutting, dyeing, permanent waving, styling, and scalp care; barbers focus on cutting, shaving, and beard trimming, and their licensing scope often covers different services; manicurists and pedicurists focus on nail services; skincare specialists focus on facial and skin care; shampooers focus on shampooing and assisting with washing and preparation; stage makeup artists focus on performance and film makeup; massage therapists focus on soft tissue massage and body care. Adjacent occupations share personal service settings, customer communication, and basic hygiene knowledge, but their core outputs, tools, and authorization requirements differ, and medical beauty procedures are undertaken by clinically authorized personnel.
Reviewable service, hygiene, and charging records

Complete cutting, dyeing, permanent waving, styling, and care according to customer requirements, and leave a record explaining the service items and the tools and products and contact times used, the skin and allergy inquiry results, tool cleaning and disinfection handling, process monitoring and result confirmation, customer feedback, charges, exceptions, and the parts that remain uncertain, so that colleagues and supervisors in the same salon can review it on that basis.
Service, hygiene, and charging records

The objects are the customer's hair and scalp and skin, tools such as scissors and clippers and combs and razors and hair dryers and curling irons and hot combs, and dyeing, permanent waving, setting, and care products; the basis is the customer's explicit requirements, product labels and instructions, the employer's and venue's hygiene and disinfection procedures, and applicable practice and occupational safety requirements.

Hairdressers, hairstylists, and cosmetologists (U.S. side O*NET 39-5012.00, Hairdressers, Hairstylists, and Cosmetologists) provide beauty services, including cutting and coloring and styling hair and massaging and treating the scalp, and may also include shampooing, applying makeup, dressing wigs, removing hair, and providing nail and skincare services. The original official duty text is “Provide beauty services, such as cutting, coloring, and styling hair, and massaging and treating scalp. May shampoo hair, apply makeup, dress wigs, remove hair, and provide nail and skincare services.”; there are 20 O*NET official tasks (14 core and 6 supplemental); core tasks include keeping the workbench clean and disinfecting tools such as scissors and combs (importance 95), scheduling customer appointments (91), bleaching and coloring and toning with applicators or brushes (90), cutting and trimming and shaping hair or hairpieces according to customer requirements and hair quality and facial features using clippers, scissors, trimmers, and razors (88), shampooing and rinsing and conditioning and drying hair and scalp or hairpieces with water and shampoo or other solutions (88), updating and maintaining customer information records (87), analyzing customers' hair and other physical features to determine and recommend beauty care or hairstyles (86), massaging and treating the scalp with hands and fingers or vibrating equipment for hygiene and therapeutic purposes (84), applying water or setting or straightening or permanent waving solutions and pressing curls with rollers, curling irons, hot combs, and curling wands (82), trimming and shaping beards (82), combing and brushing and spraying hair or wigs to set them (79), developing new styles and techniques (77), demonstrating and selling hair care products and cosmetics (76), and ordering and displaying and maintaining supplies (71); supplemental tasks include operating a cash register to receive payments (81), shaping eyebrows and removing facial hair using depilatory creams, tweezers, electrolysis, or wax (75), applying therapeutic agents as authorized and advising customers to seek medical care for chronic or infectious scalp problems (74), recommending and explaining the use of cosmetics, lotions, and creams (72), training or supervising other stylists and hairdressers and assistants (67), and fitting wigs or hairpieces on mannequins according to instructions and samples and photographs (48). This occupation is Job Zone Three in the United States (SVP 6.0 to <7.0) and is marked by O*NET as Bright Outlook. This page does not constitute dyeing or permanent waving prescriptions, contact times, or chemical handling instructions.
Communication and observation—cutting, dyeing, permanent waving, and styling—disinfection and cleaning—records

Confirm customer requirements and scalp and skin condition → verify the condition of products and tools and prepare → cut and trim and dye or curl and monitor the process → style and set and confirm the result → disinfect tools and clean the workstation → record services and products and charges and exceptions.
Reviewable service, product, and disinfection records

Service items and the tools and products and contact times used, skin and allergy inquiry results, tool cleaning and disinfection and contaminated item handling, process monitoring and result confirmation, customer feedback and charges and exceptions, and the parts that remain uncertain.
Self, colleagues in the same salon, and supervisors

Conclusions on cutting, dyeing, permanent waving, styling, and care are borne by you according to your job duties; where tool disinfection and skin barrier, chemical products and dyeing and permanent waving and formaldehyde exposure, product labels and contact times, customer skin and scalp abnormalities or allergic reactions, and determinations of scope of practice and authorization boundaries are involved, they are made by personnel with the corresponding duties and authorization in accordance with the applicable jurisdiction and the competent authority and employer systems, and when an abnormality appears or the situation exceeds your scope of practice you must stop and report.
Education and practice licensure

O*NET lists 39-5012.00 as Job Zone Three (SVP 6.0 to <7.0) and “does not publish the percentage at each education level,” listing only three categories (some jobs require a postsecondary certificate, some require a high school diploma or equivalent, and some require having attended college without a degree); the BLS Occupational Outlook Handbook lists the typical entry-level education for this occupational group as a postsecondary nondegree award, with no related work experience required and no on-the-job training, and notes that every U.S. state requires licensure, usually requiring graduation from a state-approved cosmetology or beauty program and passing an examination. The O*NET training page shows 2,285 related training programs nationwide (Cosmetology / Cosmetologist, General, Hair Styling, Salon / Beauty Salon Management, Permanent Cosmetics / Makeup and Tattooing, Make-Up Artist / Specialist, and other fields), and the Job Zone notes in the occupation summary also list example apprenticeship job titles (Cosmetologist, Hair Stylist). In mainland China, the official tasks and training background of verifiable hairdresser 4-10-03-02 can be reviewed, and specific employers' pre-job training and mentoring must have their conditions verified and must meet the applicable public place hygiene and worker health management requirements.
Do not substitute for one another

Education, occupational training, state practice licensure, employer hiring and salon authorization, and job-level authorization for chemical product and instrument use are different statuses: education and completion of training do not confer a practice license or authorization to handle chemical products and instruments; each must be verified item by item according to the state (or territory) and employer and position; the licensing scope of this occupation and barbers 39-5011.00 varies by jurisdiction, and they cannot substitute for one another.

Verify at least six items before starting: the occupational definition and employer entity (O*NET 39-5012.00 is the U.S. definition); education and occupational training; state practice license and renewal requirements; the scope of employer hiring and in-salon authorization (including whether it covers bleaching and dyeing, permanent waving, hot comb, and instrument services); venue hygiene, tool disinfection, product labels, and ventilation protection requirements; and the employment arrangement and compensation basis (hourly wage or commission or self-employment and tips).
Occupational definition

The occupational profile of the China Employment Training Technical Instruction Center specifies hairdresser 4-10-03-02: using hairdressing tools to design, trim, and create customer hairstyles, including washing, cutting, dyeing and permanent waving, hair setting, and scalp care. It can be compared with the hair services on this page, but it cannot be used to equate one-to-one with all beauty services of U.S. 39-5012. U.S. wages follow the 39-5012 wage-and-salary definition, and the combined BLS OOH chapter also contains an exact occupational sub-table; precise occupational salaries in China are still insufficient, and the industry average serves only as background.
Education and practice licensure pathway

On the U.S. side, O*NET does not publish the percentage at each education level and lists only three categories (some jobs require a postsecondary certificate, some require a high school diploma or equivalent, and some require having attended college without a degree); the BLS Occupational Outlook Handbook lists the typical entry-level education as a postsecondary nondegree award and notes that all states require licensure, usually requiring completion of a state-approved program and passing an examination; O*NET lists 2,285 related training programs and example apprenticeship job titles (Cosmetologist, Hair Stylist). The official profile of the Chinese hairdresser can serve as a task and training comparison; specific employers' pre-job training and mentoring must be verified separately and must meet the applicable public place hygiene and worker health management requirements, and specific education and experience requirements are set by the employer.
Practice and task authorization

Cutting, dyeing, permanent waving, styling, and tool disinfection must be carried out in accordance with the applicable jurisdiction and the competent authority and employer procedures; where mixing chemical products and contact times, heated tools and instruments, and the handling of customer skin and scalp abnormalities or allergic reactions are involved, this must be done within the scope of the practice license and salon authorization and escalated according to procedure. On the U.S. side, practice licensure is administered by each state and usually requires completion of a state-approved program and passing an examination; O*NET lists 3 national certifications (including laser-related certifications), none of which equals a state license or employer appointment. Verify the training and authorization process before starting, and do not infer it directly from education or experience.
Venue hygiene, tool disinfection, and chemical protection

The work environment and tools and chemicals must meet applicable hygiene and safety requirements (cleaning and disinfecting tools, handling contaminated items and chemicals and waste, cleaning workstations and floors, ventilation and lighting, heated tool protection, and protection against prolonged standing and repetitive motions). O*NET work context shows 88% continuously or almost continuously make repetitive motions, 71% continuously or almost continuously stand, 30% continuously or almost continuously bend or twist the body, 94% have face-to-face discussions every day, 88% are in contact with others continuously, 88% work very close (within touching distance) to others, 42% are exposed to contaminants every day, 38% are exposed to minor burns, cuts, bites, or stings every day, 26% are in hazardous conditions every day, 17% are exposed to disease or infections every day, and 74% wear common protective or safety equipment every day; this page does not constitute dyeing or permanent waving prescriptions, disinfection steps, or chemical handling instructions.
Shifts and working hours

Work context shows 43% face time pressure every day and 96% have a regular schedule; the typical workweek distribution is 19% exceeding 40 hours and 13% working 40 hours; 38% are in conflict situations at least once a week and 17% deal with unpleasant or angry people at least once a week; 20% consider competition extremely fierce and 22% highly fierce. The BLS Occupational Outlook Handbook notes that schedules often include evenings and weekends. When comparing positions, write the employment arrangement, commission, tips, self-employment arrangements, and overtime rules into the written terms.
Continuing training and review

Hairstyles, products, and instruments change relatively quickly; O*NET lists 6 software skills marked as hot technologies (Microsoft Office, Microsoft Excel, Microsoft Word, Apple iOS, Facebook, Intuit QuickBooks), of which the published occurrence rates for Office and Excel and Word are all below 1%; basic skills are led by active listening 72, speaking 69, critical thinking 60, and active learning 56; transferable skills are led by service orientation 66, judgment and decision making 56, social perceptiveness 53, complex problem solving 50, and time management 50; the knowledge fields publish customer and personal service 94 and sales and marketing 81. Confirm continuing education and license renewal arrangements and the salon authorization and review mechanism before starting.

All six directions share a background of personal service settings, customer communication, and basic hygiene knowledge, but their work objects, deliverable results, and licensing and authorization requirements differ; the same salon reception or service experience cannot be directly converted into a license or task authorization for another direction, medical beauty procedures are undertaken by clinically authorized personnel, and this page only compares differences in duties under public definitions.

The basis for comparison is the official occupational description of O*NET 39-5012.00 and the related occupations list on the O*NET page (including the separate adjacent code barbers 39-5011.00), as well as the adjacent occupation relationships indicated in the routing materials; an adjacent relationship only describes proximity of duties and does not mean that licenses, authorizations, or positions are interchangeable.

The table below compares hairdressers, hairstylists, and cosmetologists with five adjacent directions along the same set of dimensions: occupational direction, core work and output, key differences, and which option better suits each preference.

Barbers focus on cutting, shaving, and beard trimming, and their licensing scope often covers different services; hairdressers, hairstylists, and cosmetologists focus on comprehensive beauty services of cutting, dyeing, permanent waving, styling, and scalp care.

If you prefer cutting, shaving, and beard trimming, compare barbers first; if you prefer cutting, dyeing, permanent waving, styling, and scalp care, hairdressers, hairstylists, and cosmetologists are suitable.
Deliver cutting, dyeing, permanent waving, styling, and scalp care, with output mainly styling results and service and product records.
Hairdressers, hairstylists, and cosmetologists and barbers

Manicurists and pedicurists focus on nail shaping, decoration, and care and typically do not work on hair or dyeing and permanent waving; hairdressers, hairstylists, and cosmetologists focus on cutting, dyeing, permanent waving, and styling of hair and scalp.
If you prefer nail services, compare manicurists and pedicurists first; if you prefer hair and scalp services, hairdressers, hairstylists, and cosmetologists are suitable.
Shape, decorate, and care for nails, with output mainly nail results and service records.
Hairdressers, hairstylists, and cosmetologists and manicurists and pedicurists

Skincare specialists focus on facial and skin care and beauty treatments, but medical treatment must be undertaken by clinically authorized personnel; hairdressers, hairstylists, and cosmetologists focus on hair and scalp services, with skin care an incidental service.
If you prefer facial and skin care, compare skincare specialists first; if you prefer hair and scalp services, hairdressers, hairstylists, and cosmetologists are suitable.
Deliver facial and skin care treatments, with output mainly skin care results and customer records.
Hairdressers, hairstylists, and cosmetologists and skincare specialists

Shampooers focus on shampooing and assisting with washing and preparation and typically do not independently make dyeing, permanent waving, and styling decisions; hairdressers, hairstylists, and cosmetologists handle the complete service loop from communication to cutting, dyeing, and permanent waving to charging.

If you prefer shampooing and preparation and assistance, compare shampooers first; if you prefer handling the complete cutting, dyeing, permanent waving, and styling loop, hairdressers, hairstylists, and cosmetologists are suitable.
Perform shampooing, washing, preparation, and assistance, with output mainly washing and preparation records.
Hairdressers, hairstylists, and cosmetologists and shampooers

Stage makeup artists focus on performance, film, and stage makeup and character styling, and their work object is the makeup look and character image; hairdressers, hairstylists, and cosmetologists focus on everyday cutting, dyeing, permanent waving, styling, and care.

If you prefer performance and film makeup, compare stage makeup artists first; if you prefer everyday cutting, dyeing, permanent waving, and styling, hairdressers, hairstylists, and cosmetologists are suitable.
Complete makeup and styling according to performance or shooting requirements, with output mainly makeup and styling results.
Hairdressers, hairstylists, and cosmetologists and stage makeup artists

Massage therapists focus on soft tissue massage and body care and require a separate practice and training pathway; hairdressers, hairstylists, and cosmetologists focus on hair and scalp services, with scalp massage usually an incidental service.
If you prefer body massage and soft tissue care, compare massage therapists first; if you prefer hair and scalp services, hairdressers, hairstylists, and cosmetologists are suitable.
Perform soft tissue massage and body care according to a plan, with output mainly session records and customer feedback.
Hairdressers, hairstylists, and cosmetologists and massage therapists

Conclusion: the basis for choosing a direction is the work object, deliverable results, and licensing requirements, not whether both work in personal service settings; after choosing a direction, verify item by item the training, licensing, and task authorization requirements of the target direction.

paragraphs: Boundary: this section describes occupational risk and boundary management, not an evaluation of any individual or employer; the specific product and chemical and ventilation requirements, tool disinfection and venue hygiene, customer image and health information handling, and scope of practice and salon authorization are determined by the applicable jurisdiction, the competent authority, and employer processes. This page is based on the official duties and work context fields of O*NET 39-5012.00, and on the public content of U.S. OSHA Hair Salons: Facts about Formaldehyde in Hair Products and the U.S. FDA Cosmetics Safety Q&A.

Direct answer: the main risks include tool disinfection and skin barrier (cross-infection), chemical products and dyeing and permanent waving and formaldehyde exposure, customer image and health information leaks, repetitive motion and prolonged standing injuries, out-of-control customer and disinfection records, and unclear scope of practice and authorization; the control method is to act according to product labels and the applicable jurisdiction and the competent authority and employer procedures, and to stop and report when an abnormality appears.

O*NET supports the U.S. work context; OSHA supports the formaldehyde risk of U.S. smoothing products and employer protection requirements; China's public place hygiene regulations and the Personal Information Protection Law support the hygiene and data handling boundaries respectively. The specific scenarios and control lists are editorial synthesis, not an accident rate or a uniform operating permit.
Stylists and assistants responsible for cutting and tool cleaning and disinfection
Failure to clean and disinfect tools according to procedure may cause cross-infection between customers and between customers and practitioners.

Clean and disinfect tools such as scissors, combs, clippers, and razors according to the applicable jurisdiction and the competent authority and employer procedures, separate disposables from reusable tools, isolate potentially contaminated items, and keep handling records.
Reusing tools in an undisinfected state, or storing potentially contaminated items together with clean tools.
Stylists performing bleaching and dyeing, permanent waving, or smoothing services and the shop managers responsible for protection

Dyeing, permanent waving, setting, and smoothing products that contain formaldehyde or release it when heated may cause respiratory and eye irritation and skin allergies, and the risk of long-term exposure is higher.

For U.S. OSHA-covered settings: the employer organizes air testing, ventilation, protection, and training; practitioners verify labels and safety data and report problems, and safety cannot be judged from a “formaldehyde-free” label alone. Other jurisdictions require verification of local rules, and when an abnormality occurs, the affected step is stopped and reported according to the emergency procedures obtained.
Mixing or blending products other than according to instructions, ignoring ventilation and protection, or continuing to work when the skin is broken or abnormal.
Stylists, front desk staff, and shop managers who collect, use, or manage customer photographs and files
Sending out or improperly using customer image photographs, health information, and consumption records constitutes privacy and compliance risks.

Mainland China: customer medical and health data are sensitive personal information; verify the requirements for specific purpose, adequacy and necessity, strict protection, and separate consent in accordance with the law. Publishing photographs requires separate verification against Article 25 of the Personal Information Protection Law. Other jurisdictions must be confirmed under local rules, and in-shop authorization cannot replace a legal basis.
Sending customer photographs or health information or salon client data to unauthorized channels or using them for unauthorized purposes.
Stylists and assistants who stand continuously and cut, blow-dry, and operate heated tools
Prolonged standing, repetitive fine hand movements, and continuous close-range work may cause strain to the neck, shoulders, lower back, wrists, and thumbs.

Editorial suggestion: verify workstation and tool adjustments, rotation, and rest arrangements with your supervisor, and report discomfort promptly and seek professional advice; this page does not provide medical diagnosis or a uniform prescription.
Holding a fixed posture for long periods and working continuously under high load, or pushing through when uncomfortable.

Out-of-control service, product, disinfection, and charging records lead to unclear responsibility and difficulty tracing hygiene and product safety.

Record service items and the tools and products and contact times used, skin and allergy inquiry results, tool cleaning and disinfection and contaminated item handling, customer feedback and charges and exceptions according to procedure, explicitly flag open items, and retain traces of manual edits.

Unclear scope of practice and authorization may lead to inadequate disinfection, handling skin and scalp abnormalities on your own, or using unauthorized instruments.

Carry out services, tool disinfection, and exception handling according to the applicable jurisdiction and the competent authority and employer authorization; on the U.S. side, OSHA requires salons to conduct air testing and provide ventilation, protection, and training under the formaldehyde and hazard communication standards, and the FDA states that legal responsibility for product and ingredient safety rests with the cosmetics company and that products are managed according to the distinction between cosmetics and drugs; when a skin or scalp abnormality occurs or the situation exceeds the scope of practice, escalate according to procedure and advise seeking medical care.

subject.summary: Hairdressers, hairstylists, and cosmetologists provide beauty services: communicating with and observing the condition of hair and scalp, analyzing hair quality and face shape and recommending styling and care plans, cutting and trimming and shaping hair, shampooing and rinsing and conditioning and drying, bleaching and dyeing and toning, applying water or setting or straightening or permanent waving solutions and pressing curls with curling irons and hot combs and curling wands, massaging and treating the scalp, shaping eyebrows and removing facial hair, and keeping the workbench clean and disinfecting tools and maintaining customer information records. The U.S. side corresponds to O*NET 39-5012.00 (Hairdressers, Hairstylists, and Cosmetologists), which is Job Zone Three (SVP 6.0 to <7.0) and is marked by O*NET as Bright Outlook; barbers 39-5011.00 is a separate adjacent code, and licensing scope varies by jurisdiction. Wage, employment, and industry data are all for this occupational definition, and the page does not state that they are taken from another occupation (the BLS Occupational Outlook Handbook chapter is the combined “Barbers, Hairstylists, and Cosmetologists” definition, and this page labels them separately). On the mainland China side, this page has not obtained a public occupational entry precisely corresponding to hairdressers, hairstylists, and cosmetologists, nor a national wage distribution, so the boundary of no data that can be safely used is retained; the residents' services industry average wage cannot replace base pay and commission and tips or self-employment income, and the Chinese page language is not treated as a China equivalent occupation or wage mapping.
